stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 3-month history of limp and intermittent hip pain. Examination shows reduced hip internal rotation and abduction, with mild wasting of the thigh. Pelvic X-ray shows a flattened, fragmented femoral head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This child’s age, chronic limp, reduced hip range of motion, thigh wasting, and a flattened/fragmented femoral head on X-ray are classic for Perthes disease. Perthes typically presents between 4 and 10 years of age and causes variable limp, hip irritability, and loss of hip motion, especially internal rotation and abduction. Transient synovitis is usually a more acute, self-limited limp in younger children and does not cause femoral head flattening. Fractures and septic arthritis would have a different history and radiographic or systemic features.

citations.title: The limping or non-weight bearing child

rationale: The safest interpretation of the fragment is a Perthes disease recognition question. The existing option set already contains Perthes disease as the best answer, so the item was normalized into a complete single-best-answer question around the radiographic and clinical hallmark of Perthes disease. In children with limp, Perthes should be considered in the 4 to 10 year age group, particularly when there is reduced hip internal rotation/abduction and femoral head deformity on plain X-ray.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Perthes disease commonly presents in children aged 4 to 10 years with limp, hip pain, reduced hip motion, and X-ray changes in the femoral head
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Transient synovitis causes an acute irritable hip and usually resolves within about two weeks; it does not cause femoral head collapse or fragmentation
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect. There is no history or pattern here to suggest inflicted injury, and the X-ray description is of Perthes disease rather than fracture
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. An accidental fracture would usually follow trauma and would not explain chronic limp with flattened femoral head
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Septic arthritis is typically an acute illness with marked pain, reduced range of motion, often fever, and is an orthopaedic emergency
